central_thesis: Butterfly specialization is hierarchical and multidimensional: family-level diet breadth masks species-level host portfolios that structure geographic and anthropogenic resource opportunity, while climate independently filters the realized portion of that opportunity.

taxonomic_vs_geographic_specialization.interpretation: Taxonomic host breadth and geographic resource breadth are related but not interchangeable.

anthropogenic_resource_expansion.interpretation: Anthropogenic host redistribution expands opportunity broadly across specialists and generalists rather than preferentially releasing taxonomic generalists.

host_contribution_architecture.interpretation: Similar aggregate expansion can arise through concentrated one-host redistribution in specialists or distributed portfolio accumulation in generalists.

within_stratum_hierarchy.interpretation: Even within one host-family breadth category, species-level host richness strongly changes portfolio architecture.

independent_climate_filtering.interpretation: Climate commonly filters realized distribution within larval-resource opportunity, but filtering strength is not detectably relaxed in broader host-family generalists.

negative_results_reinterpreted.host_family_breadth_does_not_predict_pro: Family count misses the architecture of host contributions.
negative_results_reinterpreted.host_family_breadth_does_not_predict_cli: Climate acts as a separate filter rather than a simple consequence of taxonomic diet breadth.
negative_results_reinterpreted.taxonomic_vs_geographic_breadth_only_mod: Specialization contains distinct taxonomic and spatial dimensions.

paper_level_claim: The specialist-generalist continuum should be decomposed into hierarchical host taxonomy, host-species portfolio structure, spatial resource opportunity, anthropogenic opportunity architecture, and abiotic filtering rather than treated as a single ecological axis.
